@dev Unsafe write access to the balances, used by extensions that "mint" tokens using an {ownerOf} override.

 {_ownerOf} function to resolve the ownership of the corresponding tokens so that balances and ownership
 remain consistent with one another.

@dev Wrappers over Solidity's uintXX/intXX casting operators with added overflow
 checks.
 Downcasting from uint256/int256 in Solidity does not revert on overflow. This can
 easily result in undesired exploitation or bugs, since developers usually
 assume that overflows raise errors. `SafeCast` restores this intuition by
 reverting the transaction when such an operation overflows.
 Using this library instead of the unchecked operations eliminates an entire
 class of bugs, so it's recommended to use it always.

@title ClueCode
 @notice ERC-721 representing ownership of a Provider Code of the Clue Protocol
         (the numeric prefix of a Clue ID, e.g. 27 in 27-1234567890).
 Token model
  - tokenId == Provider Code read as an integer.
  - Grade S: 01-99 (2 digits), Grade A: 100-999 (3), Grade B: 10000-99999 (5).
  - Total supply is 90,999. Zero, 1000-9999 and >99999 can never be minted.
 ClueCode stores ownership only. Grade and canonical form are derived from the
 token id. Capacity, zones, links, partitions, versions and status live in
 ClueRegistry. The contract is not upgradeable and no role can transfer, burn,
 pause or re-describe a token.
 NOTE: reference implementation, not audited.
@dev Matches the pack enumeration: S = 1, A = 2, B = 3, 0 = invalid.
@notice Number of codes minted so far.
@notice True if `code` lies within a valid range.
@notice Grade of `code`; reverts with InvalidProviderCode for an invalid code.
@notice Zero-padded canonical string, e.g. 2 => "02", 100 => "100".

module that allows children to implement role-based access control mechanisms. This is a lightweight version that doesn't allow enumerating role members except through off-chain means by accessing the contract event logs. Some applications may benefit from on-chain enumerability, for those cases see {AccessControlEnumerable}. Roles are referred to by their `bytes32` identifier. These should be exposed in the external API and be unique. The best way to achieve this is by using `public constant` hash digests: ```solidity bytes32 public constant MY_ROLE = keccak256(\"MY_ROLE\"); ``` Roles can be used to represent a set of permissions. To restrict access to a function call, use {hasRole}: ```solidity function foo() public {     require(hasRole(MY_ROLE, msg.sender));     ... } ``` Roles can be granted and revoked dynamically via the {grantRole} and {revokeRole} functions. Each role has an associated admin role, and only accounts that have a role's admin role can call {grantRole} and {revokeRole}. By default, the admin role for all roles is `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, which means that only accounts with this role will be able to grant or revoke other roles. More complex role relationships can be created by using {_setRoleAdmin}. WARNING: The `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` is also its own admin: it has permission to grant and revoke this role. Extra precautions should be taken to secure accounts that have been granted it.
